title: Mesa School of Business raises Rs 110 Cr co-led by Dharana Capital and Elevation Capital
content: Mesa School of Business has raised Rs 110 crore in funding co-led Dharana Capital and existing investor Elevation Capital. This funding round is a combination of equity and debt. The equity component comprised Rs 85 crore and the venture debt of Rs 25 crore was from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital. Founded in 2023 by Ankit Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa School of Business will use this funding to build on AI-first curriculum for existing programmes, launch & grow new programmes and build strategic partnerships with the startup ecosystem. According to Mesa, it runs residential programmes built around learning by doing real things. Every student builds and runs a small business, and learns to use AI to build and launch a tech product and claims that more than 100 founders have taught on campus, and students have worked on over 200 projects with startups. Mesa is also backed by founders including Kunal Shah (CRED), Vidit Aatrey (Meesho), Abhiraj Bhal (Urban Company) and Vijay Shekhar Sharma (Paytm). “Mesa is growing quickly, but our tenets haven’t changed: every student builds something real, every student learns new age skills & AI, and founders are always in the room to give them feedback. Those tenets are why startups hire our students, and why so many of them go on to build their own startups. We believe this is the future of education for the top students.” said Ankit Agarwal, co-founder, Mesa School of Business. Mesa has grown from a single postgraduate cohort to over 550 students across three programmes in the last 3 years: a one-year Post Graduate Programme in Startup Leadership, a four-year undergraduate programme on business & entrepreneurship, and Forge, a one-year programme for fresh graduates. “The rapid evolution of modern tech has exposed a glaring disconnect in higher education: students feel unprepared for new-age roles, and companies can’t find job-ready talent. Mesa is bridging that gap by rethinking business education for an AI-first world, ensuring students develop proven, high-impact operational capabilities.” said Vamsi Duvvuri, Founder and Managing Partner, Dharana Capital.

title: Welcome to TechSparks 2026! Here’s all that’s happening on Day 1
content: Namaskara Bengaluru! India’s startup capital is officially ready for TechSparks 2026. The rules of technology are changing, and so is who gets to write them. As YourStory hosts the 17th edition of TechSparks , over the next three days at Taj Yeshwantpur, more than 10,000 attendees, 500 speakers, 1,000 startups and 300 investors will come together under this year’s theme, ‘The New Tech Order’. It is about the people, technologies and businesses shaping what comes next as AI, deep tech and new digital infrastructure change how technology is built, who can build it, and how quickly ideas can reach billions. On the inaugural day, October 13, the stage opens with Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder, Zoho, who will make the case that prosperity cannot be imported, and why genuine economic resilience requires India to build more of its underlying technology at home. Following this, YourStory will launch Tech30 2026, unveiling India’s top 30 early-stage tech innovators shaping the next decade of technology. Next, in a panel discussion, Nitin Jain (CTO, ShareChat & Moj), Ajit Narayanan (CTO, Angel One), Srividhya Srinivasan (CTO, Amagi) and Ankit Maheshwari (Founder and CTO, Innovaccer) will decode where India’s next technology advantage will come from now that talent, cost and scale are no longer enough. As the day progresses, hear Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO, AgniKul, and Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO, GalaxEye, discuss what it takes to build India’s full-stack space economy after the first launch. In a fireside chat, Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO, Angel One, will explore where the next wave of wealth will come from in India’s AI decade, and how more Indians can participate in it. In the evening, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, will be in conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory. They will discuss Karnataka’s new tech-state playbook and how India’s startup capital can learn to govern and secure new technology, not just build it. Ravi Garg, Managing Director, Enterprise Sales – APAC, Meta, will share how Meta has rebuilt its stack around AI, from Meta AI models to agents on WhatsApp and Instagram, and what that means for businesses building in India. Don’t miss Sameer Nigam, Founder and CEO, PhonePe, as he shares lessons from India’s payments decade and the blueprint for a trillion-transaction economy. The main stage wraps up with Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO, AEOS, on whether every founder needs to build an audience. Other speakers for the day include Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President, TDK Ventures; Auksė Žirgulė, VP of Product, Hostinger; Manu Saale, MD and CEO, Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India; Anjali Bansal, Partner, Avaana Capital; Anand Jain, Co-founder and CMO, CleverTap; and Rajeev Rastogi, VP – Machine Learning, Amazon, among others. Beyond the main stage, attendees can join masterclasses, hands-on Action Labs and a roundtable on the agent economy. So are you ready to dive in? Because The New Tech Order starts now!

title: Why Psychological Safety Is a High-Performance Strategy
content: Some of the most significant organisational challenges in a high-growth workplace rarely stem from a lack of technical capability. It begins with a silent choice: an engineer noticing a structural flaw during design review but choosing not to push back; a manager realising a commissioning timeline is no longer viable yet absorbing the pressure rather than escalating the risk; a junior team member withholding a critical operational insight because the perceived cost of speaking up outweighs the comfort of remaining quiet. On the surface, everything appears on track. The project milestone stays green on the executive dashboard, the meeting ends on schedule, and the targets remain unchanged. Yet, somewhere within the organisation, valuable information may not be flowing as effectively as it could. This is the hard operational reality of psychological safety. It is neither an employee perk nor a shift toward softer management. In large-scale energy and infrastructure workplaces, psychological safety is core risk management. It is the organisational capacity to surface uncomfortable truths early, before they compound into systemic failures. The Unseen Cost of Institutional Silence High-performance organisations rely on decentralised decision-making under conditions of ambiguity. In multi-gigawatt energy developments, complex engineering interfaces, tight capital allocations, and strict grid-interconnection timelines leave very little margin for error. Execution quality depends not just on individual technical mastery, but on whether that mastery can move frictionlessly across institutional hierarchies. When employees do not feel fully comfortable expressing candid perspectives, organisational efficiency and decision quality can be affected. Operational risks are flagged late in the build cycle, driving up rectification costs exponentially. Teams spend disproportionate resources correcting flawed baseline assumptions that could have been challenged at inception. According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace, employee engagement in India stands at just 23%, alongside elevated daily stress levels (28%) and workplace anxiety. AN organisation derives the greatest value from its talent only when people feel confident sharing insights, concerns, and ideas openly. Trust Is Tested in Moments of Disagreement Psychological safety cannot be engineered through corporate town halls or policy handbooks. Employees evaluate organisational trust through small, unscripted operational moments. A project review where a site engineer challenges leadership assumptions. A functional head telling the executive committee that a deadline requires recalibration. A team member owning an operational oversight before it propagates downstream. What happens in those immediate seconds dictates organisational behavior. A defensive leadership reaction may discourage future contributions. A measured, problem-solving response demonstrates that candor is a professional requirement. Managers do not merely execute strategy; they serve as the cultural filter through which organisational intent becomes daily reality. High Performance Demands High Psychological Safety There is a persistent myth that psychological safety and uncompromising operational standards exist at opposite ends of a spectrum, that driving accountability requires an environment of quiet compliance. The empirical evidence points in the opposite direction. Recent organisational research published in Frontiers in Psychiatry demonstrates a direct correlation between psychological safety, leadership trust, and workplace flourishing, even within high-stress, highly hierarchical operating environments. The research highlights that organisations are most effective when high standards are supported by high psychological safety, enabling both sustained performance and organisational agility. The objective of leadership is not to eliminate pressure, erase aggressive targets, or avoid uncomfortable conversations. Enterprises exist to deliver complex, ambitious goals. Teams will inevitably face tight timelines, market volatility, and resource constraints. The goal is to create an environment where people feel comfortable raising operational risks, seeking support when needed, and contributing their best work. A workplace capable of hearing difficult information early holds a decisive competitive advantage. It corrects courses faster, protects its capital, and retains its top talent. On the other hand, organisations that encourage open dialogue are often better positioned to identify challenges early and respond effectively. The strategic question for executive leadership extends beyond whether support programs exist on paper. The real test is whether our operating environment gives people the psychological room to voice critical truths when it matters most.

title: Tonbo Imaging’s Rs 852 Cr IPO offers investor exit
content: Tonbo Imaging India will open its Rs 852 crore initial public offering (IPO) on October 15, with a price band of Rs 665-700 per share. The issue comprises 1.22 crore existing shares offered for sale by promoters and investors, with no fresh issue. At the upper end, the company is valued at approximately Rs 4,010 crore, or about 79 times FY26 profit after tax. The offer closes on October 19, with listing expected on October 23. The IPO is primarily an exit opportunity for existing shareholders. The largest sellers are CEAQ Technologies Private Limited, offering 49.98 lakh shares, and CEAQ Technologies Pte. Ltd., offering 41.55 lakh shares. Together, they account for about 75.2% of the shares on offer. Promoters Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza will sell 11.50 lakh, 5.80 lakh and 2.30 lakh shares, respectively. Other sellers include Vinimaya Advisory LLP, Timothy Guy Mitchell, Artiman Partners and other individual and institutional investors. The selling reflects an already investor-heavy ownership structure. Before the offer, CEAQ Singapore held 25.47%, CEAQ India 8.73% and HBL Engineering 14.25%. The three promoters collectively held 17.43%. Other notable shareholders included Florintree Flowtech LLP with 5.17%, Amansa Investments with 4.25% and Yali Deeptech Fund I with 4.19%. If all offered shares are sold, the promoters’ combined stake would fall to approximately 14.01%, CEAQ India would exit its disclosed holding and CEAQ Singapore would retain about 18.22%. These are calculations based on the disclosed holdings and proposed sale quantities, rather than final post-offer figures. The Bengaluru-based company, incorporated in 2003, develops thermal imaging equipment, tactical sights and integrated defence sensor platforms. Its prospects are supported by demand for indigenous defence technology, but its financial performance remains sensitive to large contracts and delivery schedules. Revenue from operations increased 9.55% to Rs 469.08 crore in FY25 before falling 22.69% to Rs 362.65 crore in FY26. The RHP attributes the fall to “delays in the execution of certain international orders due to disruptions arising from the West Asia conflict, as well as the deferment of certain anticipated orders from Fiscal 2026 to Fiscal 2027.” The firm’s export sales fell 93.42% to Rs 20.21 crore, accounting for 5.57% of operating revenue, against Rs 307.34 crore and 65.52% in FY25. Domestic sales rose 114.89% to Rs 337.47 crore, or 93.06% of operating revenue, but could not offset the export decline. Profit after tax fell 30.07% to Rs 50.88 crore in FY26, while EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, declined 24.77% to Rs 104.62 crore. The EBITDA margin eased to 28.85% from 29.65%. The company’s operating cash flow was negative at Rs 63.22 crore in FY26, following an outflow of Rs 136.12 crore in FY25. The earlier outflow partly reflected payments for intellectual property acquired from CEAQ Singapore, while rising inventory and order timing have affected working capital. The five largest customers accounted for 53.03% of FY26 revenue, leaving the company exposed to delays or changes in a relatively small number of contracts. India’s defence exports reached Rs 38,424 crore in FY26, up 62.66% year-on-year, according to the Ministry of Defence. Paras Defence expected its exports to roughly double in FY27 amid heightened geopolitical tensions. These trends may support demand for specialised defence electronics. Tonbo’s confirmed order book stood at Rs 314.24 crore at June 2026, with another Rs 118.15 crore of orders received between July and September.

title: IndianRaga founder Sriram Emani explores identity and belonging in Jam Boy
content: Sriram Emani, the founder of IndianRaga, a global platform for Indian performing arts, has an album on Facebook showcasing all the cups he’s collected from different Starbucks outlets in New York. Each of the 74 images shows his name being misspelt. “It’s one of the most common names on the planet. But it was still spelt as ‘Syrian’, ‘Shadam’; not a single person got it right. If you can say Schwarzenegger, Saoirse Ronan, you can say Sriram,” says Emani. This frustrating experience, commonly faced by immigrants, planted the seeds for Jam Boy , Emani’s first film as a writer, director, co-producer and lead actor. Sriram Emani Jam Boy is about a model immigrant who has done everything to be chosen but has not noticed what it costs him to choose himself. Spanning 22 minutes 22 seconds, the film has already won Best Film and Best Web Series at DC Independent Film Festival, received Special Recognition at the Boston International Film Festival, and is now travelling through a growing international festival run. It will premiere on October 13 at the International Film Festival of South Asia, Toronto, North America's largest South Asian film festival. In 2012, Emani started IndianRaga while at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Fourteen years later, IndiaRaga has grown into a global performing arts organisation. Its online education programme, Raga Labs Academy, teaches Carnatic vocal music, Hindustani vocal music, Bharatanatyam, and Kathak through a structured syllabus with certification at every level. IndianRaga, headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, also offers a Raga Fellowship that selects artists through a competitive international panel to create professionally produced collaborative performances. Its artists have performed at the United Nations General Assembly, Lincoln Centre, Jacob’s Pillow, and TEDx. When Emani first spoke about IndianRaga, the platform was just beginning its journey of taking Indian classical arts to new audiences. Since then, several moments have marked its rise. When Shape of You - New Age Carnatic Mix crossed a million views in less than a day, critics who had questioned the blending of classical music with pop began to reconsider. “Maybe this actually works, and maybe this is what's required,” Emani recalls. Another defining moment was Shiva Shambho , which went on to become the world’s most-watched Bharatanatyam video online. The pandemic pushed IndianRaga to move its fellowships, collaborations, and education programmes online. Its artists have since performed at iconic venues, including Lincoln Centre, and at the World Government Summit in Dubai, where three young dancers earned an opportunity after someone in the organising team discovered their work on YouTube. South Asian stories on the global stage Emani is now embracing his own identity as an actor and filmmaker, with a desire to bring South Asian stories to the global stage. He explains, “I wanted IndianRaga to stand on its own, without my name overshadowing the brand. Over time, I realised people also wanted to know the person behind it, so I’m embracing that through acting and filmmaking, telling global stories with South Asian heritage at their centre.” Emani's foray into acting got off to a great start. “I played the first-ever South Asian Bob Cratchit in A Christmas Carol, with 20 shows for 20,000 people. We staged Tiny Tim's funeral in the Hindu tradition, and I did some Sanskrit chanting on stage,” he says. With Jam Boy , Emani is beginning to explore his next chapter, combining his experience of building a platform for South Asian arts with a larger ambition to bring South Asian stories into mainstream global entertainment. The origin of Jam Boy A still from Jam Boy Jam Boy has its roots in Emani’s experiences navigating the South Asian diaspora in the United States. He often noticed that many Indian families stayed within their communities. Children hesitated to take familiar food, such as idli-sambar, to school for fear of being told it smelled. Even accomplished professionals were reluctant to assert their cultural identity. This hesitation percolated into the performing arts space as well, he observed. After graduating from MIT, Emani spent a year hosted by 50 families across 50 cities. It shaped his understanding of how people engage with Indian performing arts beyond the stage. “For IndianRaga, I wanted to see what people think of Indian performing arts when they’re at their least guarded: at dinner table conversations, during a hectic morning, when college applications are coming up, and they have to submit an art supplement,” he says. While working as a summer intern at Lincoln Centre, he found that the Indian diaspora had no idea what they needed to present about South Asian culture on stage. “Indians are building most of the tech in North America that powers the world’s technology and leading these companies, but they are just a simple face. Nobody knows anything behind it,” he says. Hollywood was no different, Emani realised. Actors of South Asian heritage were often restricted to comic roles rather than romantic leads, detectives, or action heroes. He understood that this stemmed from the lack of stories that captured the complexity of South Asian lives. “The diversity, richness and texture I want to portray can only come if I write the story,” he says. That conviction gave rise to Jam Boy . Set in a near future where immigrant workers promised freedom are secretly indentured, Jam Boy follows an Indian coder who smuggles his mother’s forbidden tamarind rice into work and discovers why the company needs him to forget home. Emani says Jam Boy is speculative fiction that plays on the theme that the model immigrant is rewarded for being impressive. “But being impressive is not the same as being fully seen. It’s a character who’s done everything possible to be chosen, but doesn’t realise the cost of choosing himself. He’s led to believe that if he just reaches the next milestone, he can go home or get certain things. But the goalpost keeps changing, because they know model immigrants just keep working, working, working,” he elaborates. The sci-fi element in the film also lets audiences see something that might be happening in the present but isn’t being seen, by imposing boundaries through exaggerated worlds. Emani points out that the film is based on the real-life stories of many of his friends, some of whom have had to refuse promotions to protect their positions because of their H-1B visas, which keep them in technical roles. There’s also a segment about food racism that Indians experience in the US, and also internal gaslighting. “There’s a scene that resonated most with kids growing up here: the protagonist opens his pressure cooker and wants to smell the food, but he’s worried the smell will get on his shirt. So he puts on a rain poncho and comes in to work like that. Every kid from age four to 18 who has watched it says, ‘Whoa, that’s so true.’ That’s what the next generation is taking from it.” A personal connection The film also brings a deeply personal connection—Emani's mother plays his mother in Jam Boy . She has already featured in two IndianRaga videos that garnered over 2 million views across platforms. “On a spiritual level, it feels like an ancestral blessing to have my actual mom in my first film about my culture,” he says. The international premiere in Toronto is a meaningful milestone for Emani as the city has a large South Asian community. “We are waiting to get into one of the festivals in India so we can come to the country through that route first. Then I have a plan to release it online next year,” he says. Meanwhile, the short film is opening doors to larger possibilities: a feature-length version of Jam Boy . He is now working with the Rickshaw Film Foundation’s writers’ room to revise the script while exploring a web series adaptation. Beyond Jam Boy , Emani is developing thrillers that place South Asian protagonists in global settings. As a Trust and Storytelling Fellow at Boston University, his mission is to use storytelling devices to build trust in institutions and people. “I’m calling my umbrella Ancestors and Algorithms . It examines what we inherit and what happens to it as the world around us changes: inheritance through migration, technology, and cultural change,” he says. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Ecomm festive sales hit Rs 24,000 Cr in two days; VC funding drops as large deals dry up
content: Dear Reader, India’s ecommerce platforms clocked around Rs 24,000 crore in sales during the first two days of festive shopping, with mobile phones accounting for the largest share by value, according to Redseer Strategy Consultants. Around 6-6.5 crore shoppers placed 8-9 crore orders, with demand extending to electronics, appliances and fashion, particularly among consumers in Tier II cities and smaller towns. India’s digital infrastructure is also drawing attention, with Elon Musk vowing to make Starlink affordable in the country. The move could set up a contest with Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio, as both companies await government clearance for their satellite internet services, days before Jio Platforms’ planned $106 billion IPO. As AI adoption accelerates, questions around safety and accountability are coming to the fore. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for an “emergency brake” for advanced AI models , urging companies to assume these systems could be compromised and build safeguards from the outset. He wants human-controlled shutdown mechanisms, independent audits and tamper-proof records of AI actions to ensure transparency and accountability as AI agents become more autonomous. The push for stronger safeguards is also bringing independent AI safety evaluators into focus. As OpenAI and Anthropic face growing pressure to subject their models to third-party audits, concerns persist over evaluators’ funding, access to sensitive systems and ability to operate independently, fuelling calls for greater government oversight. title: Zetwerk sets IPO price band at Rs 143-151, aims to raise Rs 5,012 Cr
content: Zetwerk, the Bengaluru-headquartered manufacturing marketplace, has set a price band of Rs 143–151 per share for its initial public offering (IPO), targeting a valuation of Rs 25,583 crore. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares and an offer for sale (OFS). The company has expanded the size of the public issue to Rs 5,012 crore. The fresh issue has been increased from Rs 2,600 crore to Rs 2,830 crore, while the OFS component has been expanded from 9.68 crore shares to 14.45 crore shares. Early investors, including Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, and Kae Capital, have increased the number of shares they plan to sell. The proposed share sale by the founders remains unchanged. Lightspeed Venture Partners plans to sell 2.51 crore shares, followed by Peak XV Partners with 2.34 crore shares and Accel India with 1.2 crore shares. Zetwerk’s promoters, Amrit Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, will sell 1.42 crore shares, while promoter group entity Creovate Innovation will offload 2.30 crore shares. The IPO will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. The anchor investor book will open on October 14, and the shares are expected to list on the stock exchanges on October 23. Zetwerk plans to use around Rs 2,160 crore from the fresh issue to repay debt. The remaining proceeds will be allocated towards acquisitions, strategic investments and general corporate purposes. The company reported revenue of Rs 15,913 crore in FY26, a 40.4% increase from Rs 11,332 crore in FY25. However, its losses widened to Rs 1,606.2 crore in FY26 from Rs 370.7 crore in the previous fiscal year, largely due to a one-time charge. Established in 2017, Zetwerk is a digital manufacturing marketplace that connects businesses, manufacturers and suppliers on one platform. In Q1 FY27, its revenue from operations grew 55% year-on-year to Rs 4,118 crore, while losses from continuing operations narrowed to Rs 64 crore from Rs 881 crore in the year-ago quarter.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 12, 2026)
content: From ShuruKar, billed as the first nationwide district-level movement of its kind that aims to help young Indians identify a problem worth solving in their district, to India’s ecommerce platforms recording around Rs 24,000 crore in sales during the first two days of festive shopping, here are the latest developments across sectors . Featured Stories ShuruKar: Your next business could start in your hometown A big idea does not need a big city. That was the message from Patna, where The Bharat Project, an initiative by YourStory, launched ShuruKar at Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam Science City in Rajinder Nagar. Developed in partnership with DPIIT and Startup India, ShuruKar is billed as the first nationwide district-level movement of its kind. title: 5 Must-read lessons from Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly
content: Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important part of everyday life, changing how people work, communicate, and form relationships. But beyond questions of productivity and technological disruption lies a more personal concern: how might AI reshape human emotions, companionship, and our understanding of what it means to be alive? In Endless Dream , speculative fiction writer Gigi Ganguly explores these questions through interconnected stories set across different points in the future. The novel imagines societies where humans and artificial intelligence coexist in increasingly complex ways, examining themes such as AI companionship, grief, digital existence, loneliness, and belonging. Rather than presenting technology as an uncomplicated solution to human problems or an inevitable threat, Ganguly uses imagined futures to explore the emotional and ethical questions that accompany technological progress. 5 Powerful lessons from Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly to reflect on 1. Human connection goes beyond technology Technology can make communication easier, connect people across distances, and offer new forms of companionship. Yet the ability to communicate does not automatically guarantee that we feel understood or emotionally connected. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly sophisticated, the boundaries between human interaction and digital companionship may become more complicated. AI systems might offer conversation, familiarity, and comfort, but questions about the nature of these relationships will remain. Endless Dream invites readers to consider what makes a connection meaningful. The lesson is that genuine connection involves more than constant communication. It requires us to think about trust, emotional understanding, vulnerability, and the needs that relationships fulfil in our lives. 2. Grief cannot always be resolved through technology Grief is one of the most deeply personal experiences of being human. Losing someone can leave behind questions, memories, and a longing to reconnect with a person who is no longer physically present. In a future shaped by advanced artificial intelligence and digital existence, technology might offer new ways to preserve memories or recreate aspects of a person's presence. Such possibilities could provide comfort, but they could also raise difficult questions about acceptance and letting go. Would a digital recreation of someone we have lost help us process our grief, or make it harder to accept their absence? Could a simulation ever replace the complexity of a relationship shared with a living person? These questions highlight the difference between preserving someone's digital traces and understanding the emotional reality of losing them. The lesson is not that technology has no place in the grieving process. Rather, it encourages us to consider the limits of technological solutions when dealing with experiences that are fundamentally emotional and personal. Also Read 5 Comforting books for grief, heartbreak, and hard times 3. Progress raises new ethical questions Technological advancement is often measured by what becomes possible. New systems can perform tasks more efficiently, expand human capabilities, and introduce entirely new ways of living. However, the fact that something can be developed does not automatically mean that it should be used without careful consideration. As artificial intelligence becomes more integrated into society, questions about responsibility, autonomy, privacy , and the treatment of non-human intelligence become increasingly important. The possibilities imagined in speculative fiction allow readers to examine these concerns before they become familiar features of everyday life. Endless Dream creates space to consider how societies might respond when technological capabilities challenge existing moral assumptions. The lesson is that progress requires more than innovation. It also demands thoughtful decisions about how new capabilities should be developed, governed, and used. 4. The search for belonging remains important The world around us may change dramatically, but the desire to feel accepted and understood remains an important part of human experience. People seek belonging through friendships, families, communities, and shared experiences. Yet loneliness can persist even in environments where communication is constant and opportunities to interact are abundant. In futures where artificial intelligence becomes a regular presence in personal and social life, the meaning of belonging may become more complicated. Digital companionship might provide comfort, while new forms of existence could challenge traditional ideas about identity and community. These possibilities encourage readers to think about whether belonging depends on shared biology, common experiences, emotional understanding, or something more difficult to define. The lesson is that technological convenience cannot, by itself, answer every question about loneliness and identity. Understanding what makes us feel connected to others remains essential, regardless of how society evolves. 5. Being human means living with uncertainty One of the defining characteristics of speculative fiction is its ability to imagine futures that challenge familiar assumptions. By placing recognisable emotions and dilemmas in unfamiliar circumstances, it allows readers to reconsider ideas they might otherwise take for granted. Artificial intelligence, digital existence, and the possibility of radically different ways of living raise questions that do not always have simple answers. The boundaries between human and machine, presence and absence, or memory and identity may become increasingly difficult to define. Instead of offering definitive solutions to every dilemma, stories about possible futures can encourage readers to remain curious and open to different perspectives. Endless Dream invites reflection on what it means to live in a world where the familiar rules of existence may no longer apply in the same way. The lesson is that uncertainty does not always need to be eliminated. Sometimes, acknowledging what we do not yet understand is the first step towards making more thoughtful decisions about the future. Final thoughts Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly explores how AI could shape human relationships and future societies. Through themes of grief, belonging, connection and ethical innovation, the novel invites readers to reflect on what gives life meaning. As AI evolves, these questions become more relevant. Technology may change how we communicate and experience the world, but imagining the future also means considering the values and human connections we want to preserve.

title: 5 Lessons from The Average Advantage by Utsav Malhotra
content: What if you could build a successful career without constantly trying to be the best, working longer hours or making sure everyone knows how ambitious you are? In a world where professionals are encouraged to hustle harder, dream bigger and build impressive personal brands, the pressure to stand out can become exhausting. Social media often makes success look like a race in which everyone is moving ahead, landing better jobs, earning more money and achieving extraordinary things. Meanwhile, the everyday work that keeps businesses running rarely receives the same attention. Utsav Malhotra challenges this idea of success. Drawing on more than two decades of experience in Indian corporate life, Malhotra explores why being average does not necessarily mean being mediocre and why consistent effort can matter more than occasional brilliance. As the Chief Operating Officer at Noise, Malhotra has spent years navigating the realities of business, from brand-building and strategy to fundraising and organisational challenges. His debut book offers a different perspective for professionals who want to do meaningful work without turning their entire lives into a pursuit of professional recognition. 5 Lessons from The Average Advantage on success without the hustle 1. Being average is not the same as being mediocre Society often encourages us to stand out, be the best and achieve extraordinary things. However, not everyone needs to be at the top to make a valuable contribution. Malhotra distinguishes between being average and being mediocre. Being average is simply part of life, while mediocrity involves a lack of effort to improve. Someone who consistently delivers good work, supports colleagues and learns from mistakes can be valuable without being the most celebrated person in the room. The lesson: Focus on doing your work well instead of constantly comparing yourself with others. You do not have to be exceptional at everything to build a successful career. 2. Small efforts can create lasting success Success rarely happens overnight. More often, it develops through small improvements that accumulate over time. Malhotra highlights the importance of compounding, whether in professional skills, relationships, reputation or financial stability. For instance, a writer who regularly improves their research and storytelling skills may not produce a groundbreaking article every day. However, consistent practice can make them better over the years. The same principle applies to almost every area of life. Small actions may seem insignificant initially, but their long-term impact can be substantial. The lesson: Do not underestimate ordinary efforts. Focus on improving a little every day and give your progress enough time to compound. 3. Your career does not have to define your entire life We are often told to follow our passion and make our work our biggest source of fulfilment. But constantly chasing professional goals can leave little room for family, friendships, hobbies and rest. Malhotra questions the pressure to make work the centre of our identity. You can enjoy your profession, work towards meaningful goals and still have interests outside your career. A successful life does not necessarily mean being available around the clock or thinking about work long after the day ends. Sometimes, having the freedom to enjoy life beyond your job is an achievement in itself. The lesson: Build a career that supports the life you want. Your professional achievements matter, but they are only one part of who you are. Also Read ‘Being powerful is having the ability to empower others’ – 20 quotes of the week on leaders and entrepreneurs 4. Focus on meaningful work, not constant visibility Modern workplaces often reward visibility through networking, personal branding and frequent displays of achievement. While communicating your work is important, constantly trying to prove your value can become exhausting. The Average Advantage questions whether these corporate habits always contribute to better results. Instead of spending all your energy appearing busy or ambitious, it encourages you to focus on competence, judgment and dependable work. Being someone others can trust to deliver on commitments may contribute more to your long-term reputation than constantly promoting yourself. The lesson: Let your work speak through its quality, while communicating your contributions when necessary. You do not have to turn every achievement into a performance. 5. Define success on your own terms A high salary, prestigious job title or rapid promotion may represent success to one person but not necessarily to another. The problem begins when we pursue these milestones simply because society expects us to. Malhotra encourages readers to think about what they are actually building. Along with professional growth, consider whether your health, relationships, financial freedom and personal well-being are improving. For some people, success means leading a large team. For others, it means doing meaningful work while having enough time for their families. Neither definition is automatically better than the other. The lesson: Choose goals that reflect your values rather than someone else's expectations. Ambition becomes more meaningful when it leads towards a life you genuinely want. Final thoughts The Average Advantage by Utsav Malhotra offers a refreshing reminder that success does not require extraordinary performance every single day. Consistency, competence and good judgment can be just as valuable as moments of brilliance. The book does not ask readers to abandon ambition. Instead, it encourages them to pursue it sustainably, without getting caught up in the pressure to constantly stand out. Sometimes, the most meaningful progress comes from showing up, doing the work and allowing ordinary efforts to create extraordinary results over time

title: The Zocket Story: Building Brand Brain, the context and orchestration layer for AI-native enterprise marketing
content: When Zocket was founded in India in 2021, the company began with a focused ambition: make digital marketing significantly easier for businesses. What followed was a much larger journey. As Zocket moved deeper into marketing, worked with increasingly complex organizations, and watched artificial intelligence reshape the industry, the problem it set out to solve evolved. What began as an effort to simplify digital advertising became a much bigger question: How should modern enterprises run marketing in the AI era? Answering that question meant looking beyond individual tools and isolated AI use cases. It meant rethinking how brand knowledge, consumer intelligence, creative, media, and governance could operate as one connected system, with AI carrying the context of the brand across decisions and orchestrating action across marketing workflows. In 2026, Zocket evolved from a self-serve advertising platform to an enterprise AI company working with consumer brands to build the context and orchestration layer for AI-native marketing. Today, Zocket works with 100+ enterprise brands across 25+ countries. At the center of this proposition is Brand Brain, a shared intelligence layer designed to understand brand, consumer, and business context, and make that intelligence available across marketing workflows. From digital advertising to enterprise marketing AI Zocket was founded by Karthik Venkateswaran, Nandha Kumar Ravi, Sundar Natesan, and Mukund Srivathsan, a founding team that had already spent years building together. Before Zocket, the four built GoBumpr, a technology platform connecting vehicle owners with automobile service providers, which they scaled across multiple Indian cities before exiting the business in 2021. That experience gave the team a firsthand understanding of building a consumer business in an increasingly digital economy. Customer acquisition was becoming more important, but reaching and engaging consumers was also becoming increasingly complex. Zocket initially focused on simplifying that complexity. Its platform brought together more than 150 variables to inform decisions around creative, copy, targeting, and channels. The company subsequently raised a $3 million seed round led by Kalaari Capital , with participation from Kettleborough VC. But as Zocket began working more deeply within marketing, the team realized that the larger problem was not any single marketing activity. It was the fragmentation surrounding it. Zocket Founders Why AI needs more than a prompt Generative AI has dramatically reduced the time required to create content, analyze information, and produce marketing recommendations. But enterprise marketing requires something models do not inherently possess: the context of the brand. A brand is not simply a logo, prompt, or guideline document. It is the accumulation of campaigns, consumer interactions, product knowledge, creative history, performance data, market intelligence, regulatory requirements, and organizational decisions. For AI to become useful at enterprise scale, it needs to understand that context. It needs to know how a brand communicates, what consumers are saying, which claims are approved, what has worked previously, what cannot be said, and where human intervention is required. And context alone is not enough. That intelligence must be orchestrated across marketing workflows , allowing consumer signals to inform creative, creative to connect with paid media, performance to influence subsequent decisions, and governance to remain consistent throughout. This became the foundation for Brand Brain . Brand Brain: From fragmented data to shared intelligence Brand Brain is Zocket's shared intelligence layer designed to give AI persistent context about a brand's identity, consumers, guidelines, campaigns, performance, and governance rules. Rather than treating consumer intelligence, brand guidelines, creative history, customer conversations, and campaign performance as disconnected inputs, Brand Brain brings relevant signals together and interprets them within the context of the enterprise. The objective is not simply to aggregate more data. Enterprises already have enormous amounts of it. The challenge is determining what information matters, how different signals relate, and how that context should influence the next action. A change in consumer sentiment can influence messaging. Campaign performance can inform the next creative decision. Brand guidelines establish boundaries for what AI can generate. Market signals can influence how and where campaigns are activated. This creates a continuous intelligence loop: Signals → Context → Intelligence → Execution → Outcomes → Learning Zocket extends this intelligence across six specialized marketing modules: Tasks, AI Designer, Brand Moderator, Consumer Insights, AI Paid Media, and Reporting. Brand Brain sits across these modules as the shared context layer , allowing each capability to operate from a common understanding of the brand rather than starting from an isolated prompt. Zocket's Home experience acts as the prompt router, directing intent into the relevant workflows while Brand Brain maintains the underlying context. As Karthik Venkateswaran , Co-founder and CEO, Zocket, explains: “Enterprise marketing does not need another AI tool operating in isolation. It needs AI that understands the context of the brand and can orchestrate that intelligence across marketing. “That is what we are building with Brand Brain: a shared context and orchestration layer for how enterprise consumer brands run marketing in an AI-native era.” Building AI for enterprise scale For enterprise brands, intelligence and automation also need governance. Large organizations operate across products, sub-brands, markets, and regulatory environments. Communication approved for one product may not be appropriate for another, while certain marketing decisions may require legal, compliance or brand approval. Zocket's enterprise approach combines intelligence and orchestration with controls around permissions, approvals, brand rules, and traceability. Teams can determine where AI can act, where human approval is required and where actions need to be escalated, creating a human-in-the-loop approach to consequential marketing decisions. Mukund Srivathsan , Co-founder and CTO, Zocket, says the model is not the moat and the real challenge is building the context around it. “Brand Brain brings together brand knowledge, consumer signals, performance history and governance, and makes that intelligence available to every AI workflow. That is what allows AI to move from generating isolated outputs to making more informed, connected marketing decisions at enterprise scale,” he says. The value of enterprise AI is therefore not determined only by what it can generate. It is determined by whether an organization can govern it, control it, and reliably apply it across marketing workflows. From enterprise adoption to industry recognition The shift is increasingly reflected in Zocket's enterprise footprint. Today, the company works with 200+ enterprise brands across 25+ countries, including consumer brands such as Bata and Dabur, applying AI across areas including consumer intelligence, creative, paid media, and brand governance. In 2026, Zocket's approach was recognized through the Accenture Tech Next Challenge 2026, where it was named a winner for its work around AI-native marketing and autonomous growth. Zocket also won Best Use of AI in Media & Entertainment at the ET Enterprise AI Awards 2026, reflecting its growing focus on bringing context-aware AI into real enterprise marketing workflows. For Zocket, these milestones represent a very different company from the one that began by simplifying digital advertisements five years ago. But the underlying principle remains the same: technology should remove complexity from marketing rather than create more of it. The next chapter The next phase of enterprise AI will not be defined simply by how much content brands can generate or how many tasks they automate. It will be defined by how effectively organizations connect context, intelligence, and action while maintaining the governance and control their brands require. Consumer intelligence should inform creativity. Creative should connect with paid media. Performance should contribute to what happens next. Brand and compliance rules should remain present throughout the process. That is the future Zocket is building toward. What began as a question about making digital marketing easier has evolved into a much more ambitious one: How should enterprise consumer brands run marketing in an AI-native era? For Zocket, the answer lies in giving AI the context of the brand and orchestrating that intelligence across marketing. To learn more, visit www.zocket.com

title: The Wealth Company AIF invests Rs 400 Cr in Boldfit
content: The Wealth Company Alternates has announced that its Bharat Value Fund, a Category II AIF, has invested approximately Rs 400 crore in Boldfit, a homegrown sports brand, as part of its Series B funding round. A statement said that the investment will support Boldfit’s next phase of expansion, with investments planned for nationwide retail expansion, product innovation and manufacturing. The company will also selectively pursue inorganic opportunities to strengthen its category presence and capabilities. Founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani, Boldfit had previously raised Rs 110 crore from global venture capital firm Bessemer Venture Partners in its Series A funding round in 2024. The company also counts prominent Indian sportspersons KL Rahul and Sania Mirza among its investors. Boldfit Founder and CEO Pallav Bihani said, “We’re building a deeply integrated sports business, investing in product innovation, manufacturing excellence and nationwide retail to create the scale and capabilities required to serve India’s sporting ambitions.” This is the fourth investment by Bharat Value Fund in the past 12 months, with an average deal value of around Rs 400 crore each. “ India is undergoing a fundamental shift in how it engages with fitness and sports. Active living is no longer confined to a facility or occasional play- it is transitioning into a frequent, daily household habit across the country. Pallav has achieved what few direct-to-consumer founders are able to manage - rapid, category-defining scale anchored by profitability. Our investment reflects our conviction in the company’s growth potential and our approach of partnering with businesses that have the ability to build enduring scale and long-term value," Madhu Lunawat, Founder and Whole-time Director, Wealth Company Asset Management Private Limited, said. According to the statement, Boldfit serves over two crore customers annually and has grown at a CAGR of 80%+ for the last three years. India’s fitness and sports goods market is estimated at approximately $16 billion and projected to grow at a CAGR of over 16% reaching $35 billion by FY31 underpinned by rising disposable incomes, a young population, growing health awareness and the mainstreaming of active lifestyles and athleisure.

title: 5 Must-read books that teach you how to think independently
content: Independent thinking is a skill that has become increasingly valuable in a world filled with constant opinions, trends, and information. From social media feeds to workplace expectations, people are often encouraged to follow the crowd rather than question it. Yet some of the most meaningful ideas, innovations, and personal breakthroughs come from individuals who learn to think for themselves. Books can play an important role in developing this ability. The right book can challenge your assumptions, expose you to new perspectives, and encourage you to examine your beliefs more carefully. Whether through philosophy, psychology, or practical wisdom, these titles offer valuable lessons on how to become a more independent thinker. 1. Think Again by Adam Grant Many people view changing their minds as a sign of weakness. Adam Grant argues the opposite. In Think Again , he explores the importance of rethinking our assumptions and remaining open to new evidence. Drawing on research and real-life examples, Grant shows how intellectual flexibility can lead to better decisions and stronger relationships. One of the book's central ideas is that independent thinkers are not those who stubbornly hold onto their beliefs but those who are willing to question them. By encouraging readers to embrace curiosity and uncertainty, Think Again offers practical tools for developing a more thoughtful and independent mindset. 2. Meditations by Marcus Aurelius Written nearly two thousand years ago, Meditations remains one of the most influential books on personal reflection and self-mastery. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius recorded his thoughts on dealing with challenges, emotions, and societal pressures. Throughout the book, he emphasises the importance of focusing on what you can control rather than being influenced by external opinions. His reflections encourage readers to develop inner confidence and rely on reason rather than public approval. The book remains a powerful guide for anyone seeking to think independently while maintaining a sense of balance and purpose. 3. The Demon-Haunted World by Carl Sagan Carl Sagan's classic work is a passionate defence of scientific thinking and scepticism. In The Demon-Haunted World , Sagan explains why critical thinking is essential for separating facts from misinformation. He introduces readers to tools that can help evaluate claims, identify faulty reasoning, and resist manipulation. The book is especially relevant in today's information-rich environment, where misleading claims can spread quickly. Sagan's emphasis on evidence-based thinking makes this an excellent read for anyone looking to strengthen their ability to form independent conclusions. 4. Walden by Henry David Thoreau When Henry David Thoreau moved to a small cabin near Walden Pond, he embarked on an experiment in simple living that would inspire generations of readers. In Walden , Thoreau reflects on nature, society, and the pursuit of a meaningful life. He questions conventional definitions of success and encourages readers to examine whether they are living according to their own values or simply following social expectations. The book's message remains relevant today, offering a reminder that independent thinking often begins with the courage to step away from the crowd and reflect on what truly matters. Also Read 7 Books that teach you how to think under pressure 5. The Courage to Be Disliked by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga Based on the ideas of psychologist Alfred Adler, this bestselling book explores what it means to live authentically. Presented as a conversation between a philosopher and a young student, The Courage to Be Disliked challenges common beliefs about happiness, relationships, and personal freedom. The authors argue that many people allow fear of judgment to shape their choices. The book encourages readers to take responsibility for their lives and make decisions based on their values rather than the expectations of others. Its practical insights make it a compelling guide to independent thought and self-determination. Final thoughts Independent thinking is not about rejecting every popular idea or always being different. It is about developing the ability to evaluate information carefully, question assumptions, and make decisions that align with your own understanding and values. Books like Think Again , Meditations , The Demon-Haunted World , Walden , and The Courage to Be Disliked offer valuable lessons in critical thinking, self-reflection, and intellectual independence. Together, they provide a strong foundation for anyone seeking to navigate the world with greater confidence, clarity, and originality.

title: Ecommerce firms sell goods worth Rs 24k Cr in first two days of festive sales: Redseer
content: Ecommerce firms are estimated to have sold goods worth around Rs 24,000 crore in the first two days of the festive season sale, driven by growth in order volumes, with mobile phones accounting for the biggest share in value terms, according to consultancy firm Redseer Strategy Consultants. The consultancy firm estimated that shoppers placed about 8-9 crore orders across all platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Ajio and many other marketplaces. Redseer Strategy Consultants, Associate Partner, Nikhil Dalal told PTI that the first two days pointed to India's festive e-commerce basket getting wider. The growth is being led by order volumes, with consumers spreading spend beyond mobiles into fashion, electronics and appliances as well. "Value fashion stood out, as shoppers from Tier 2 and smaller towns bought festive wear at accessible price points. The first two days saw over USD 2.5 billion (close to Rs 24,200 crore) in GMV, and around 60-65 million shoppers have already participated in the first two days," he said. The growth in GMV (gross merchandise value) was around 6 times the business-as-usual (BAU) daily run rate, the firm said. Players like Amazon and Flipkart are using their quick commerce arms for sales and increasing their salience on the platform, which saw 4 to 5 times higher GMV than the BAU daily average. Sales of large appliances and electronics grew faster than the market, even as mobiles remained the largest category by value, according to the estimates. Mobile phones are estimated to have accounted for 38-40 per cent or about Rs 9,100-9,600 crore of total sales. Redseer estimates consumer electronics share in total sales to be around 25-27 per cent, or Rs 6,000-6,500 crore and fashion products in the range of 15-18 per cent, or about Rs 3,630-4,350 crore. The 55-inch TV upgrade, large appliances and electronics together contributed approximately 25-27 per cent of GMV. TVs, refrigerators, and ACs accounted for more than two-thirds of the large-appliance sales. Models with 55-inch screens from TCL, LG, Samsung and Xiaomi represented more than 75 per cent of the top-selling TV SKUs. According to Redseer's estimate, electronics had already grown by more than 20 per cent in the first half of 2026, partly as consumers brought purchases forward amid expectations of higher prices in the second half of 2026. The first two days of festive sales still recorded around 14 times more orders than average BAU, led by laptops and IoT devices in electronics. Fashion GMV grew 22-25 per cent year-on-year in the first two days, making 15-18 per cent share of the total GMV and about 3 to 5 times its BAU average GMV. Gen Z accounted for approximately one-third of opening-day shoppers, according to Redseer estimates. Of an estimated 6-6.5 crore shoppers who purchased during the first two days, Redseer estimates that around two-thirds of them came from Tier 2 and rural areas. Approximately 15-16 crore unique shoppers typically transact across e-commerce platforms in a business-as-usual month. "The opening two days therefore brought over one-third of this monthly shopper base into the festive sale. First-time shoppers doubled from last year. "We expect 100 million shoppers to shop in the entire 11-day first leg," Dalal said.

title: UP cabinet approves startup procurement scheme
content: The Uttar Pradesh Cabinet has approved the Uttar Pradesh Startup Procurement Scheme - 2026. The scheme aims to facilitate market access for eligible startups in the state and promote the use of their innovative products, services and solutions by government departments and other agencies, the UP government said in a statement. Under the scheme, a dedicated UP Startup E-Marketplace will be established to list innovative products, services and solutions developed by eligible startups and facilitate their procurement by government departments. This platform will enable government departments to procure innovative products and services offered by startups. The departments will make purchases from their approved budgetary provisions. The Uttar Pradesh Startup Mission will be responsible for establishing, operating and maintaining the UP Startup E-Marketplace, ensuring its continued implementation. The wider use of these technological solutions will improve the quality, efficiency and accessibility of government services. Citizens will directly benefit from better, more effective and accessible service delivery. Under the scheme, eligible innovative enterprises registered under the Uttar Pradesh Startup Policy will also have opportunities to secure work orders from government departments. Access to government procurement opportunities will encourage business expansion among startups and generate additional direct and indirect employment opportunities in the state, the statement added. The Uttar Pradesh government also approved a skill training and employment development scheme to make the state a key sourcing hub for skilled manpower and a “global manpower hub”. The Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Skill Training and Employment Zone Development Scheme was approved by the state cabinet. Under the scheme, it will develop an integrated skill training and employment ecosystem across nine zones, covering all 75 districts. This will help train young people to meet industry requirements and connect them with employment opportunities in India and abroad. The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector plays an important role in Uttar Pradesh's industrial development. The state has approximately 96 lakh MSME enterprises, accounting for 14.2 per cent of the country's approximately 6.77 crore enterprises.

title: Amazon, Flipkart see strong start to 2026 festive sales
content: India’s two largest ecommerce platforms, Amazon India and Flipkart, have launched their flagship annual festive sales—the Amazon Great Indian Festival (GIF) 2026 and Flipkart’s The Big Billion Days (TBBD) 2026. Both platforms reported strong consumer participation, sharp increase in demand across categories, and growing adoption of quick-commerce delivery options in non-metro markets. Scale, traffic, and reach Amazon said it recorded over 440 million visits during the opening phase of its sale, the highest volume in its history. The platform saw a 100% year-on-year increase in products ordered, while daily app downloads surged fivefold. More than 72% of visits came from outside the top nine metros. First-time shoppers nearly doubled year-on-year, and orders were placed from every pin code in the country. Flipkart, meanwhile, recorded 6.3 million concurrent users per minute during its opening peak hour, attracting over six times as many active users as during a regular hour. The platform said it also recorded 287 million sessions during the early access window for Plus, Black, and co-branded card members. Non-metro markets accounted for approximately 60% of overall traction, with Tier III towns and beyond contributing nearly half of all visits during the opening hour, it said. New customer numbers grew 34% during the same period. Category drivers and shopping trends Amazon said electronics and premium upgrades performed exceptionally well. Premium Android smartphone sales rose 70% year-on-year, while MacBook Neo sales grew 65X over a regular business day. Large appliances surged 50X, led by washing machines (80X), refrigerators (60X), and home entertainment (77X). In fashion, footwear sales reached seven pairs per second, while Nike sales rose 16-fold compared with regular days. Denim sales exceeded 1,500 pairs per hour, while premium beauty products sold at a rate of 150 units per minute. Flipkart said it saw strong demand in Large Appliances, which grew 30% year-on-year in the first hour, alongside a 73% year-on-year jump in tablets. Beauty sales on Flipkart grew 42% overall and 48% among Gen Z shoppers, heavily propelled by men's grooming. At peak, Flipkart said it processed over 1,600 units of men's perfume every minute. On the engagement side, over 12.7 million users accessed Flipkart’s live commerce and video shopping experiences, while 64% of Voice Search users came from Tier II plus markets. Quick commerce and digital payment adoption Rapid fulfillment became a central battleground across both marketplaces. Amazon said it fulfilled orders within minutes across more than 120 cities served by Amazon Now. Flipkart Minutes saw order volumes rise 3.5X over normal days and new customers jump 11X in the first hour, highlighted by a record delivery of an iPhone 17 to a customer in New Delhi in 3.4 minutes. Affordability levers drove high-ticket conversion across both platforms. Half of Amazon’s buyers utilised EMI options, while Amazon Pay Later saw transactions double and its user base expand by 80% year-on-year. Flipkart similarly reported that one in three mobile buyers opted for No Cost EMI, while one in four utilized product exchange offers. Merchant ecosystem and brand traction Seller participation expanded across both platforms. Amazon said sellers recorded over 2X units ordered in the first 24 hours compared to last year, with sellers generating over Rs 1 crore in sales growing by more than 80%. Category growth for sellers was led by beauty (7X), kitchen (4.2X), and wireless (3.4X). Some of the key partner brands reported significant surges such as Philips (10X over daily baseline), Reebok (doubled sales YoY), WROGN (10X over daily baseline), and Penguin Random House India (up nearly 50% YoY). Flipkart said reported that 51% of transacting sellers doubled their standard daily business during Early Access. Sellers based in Tier II plus regions such as small businesses and MSMEs achieved a 2.9X growth, with manufacturing and seller hubs such as Bhiwandi, Panipat, Tirupur, and Hisar leading the sales momentum.

title: Lalit Kala Akademi features 270 artworks in its 65th National Exhibition of Art

For over six decades, India's National Academy of Art has provided a platform for contemporary artistic expression. As seen in this photo essay, the exhibition celebrates the creative excellence of Indian artists and reflects the evolving visual culture of Indian traditions and contemporary practices. Viewers from India and overseas are inspired by the shared values and cultural imagination of a living civilisation with ancient roots. Examples include Bengal's scroll traditions, southern sculpture practices, and the distinctive artistic traditions of the North-East. For artists, being featured at the exhibition provides national visibility and institutional recognition. For audiences, it offers a broad survey of current artistic practices across geographical and stylistic boundaries.
